children.text: This Catholic cathedral in the La Huerta district of Parañaque began as a 16th-century Augustinian mission parish dedicated to St. Andrew, and today it is the seat of the Diocese of Parañaque. It is a diocesan shrine housing the image of Our Lady of Buen Suceso, and it is within walking distance of LRT-1 Ninoy Aquino station.
The full name of St. Andrew Cathedral in Parañaque is
Cathedral Parish of St. Andrew
, and as a diocesan shrine it also goes by
Nuestra Señora del Buen Suceso (Our Lady of the Good Event)
. It stands in La Huerta, the old center of Parañaque City in southern Metro Manila, on Quirino Avenue. The Diocese of Parañaque was carved out of the Archdiocese of Manila by Pope John Paul II on
December 7, 2002
and covers three cities: Parañaque, Las Piñas and Muntinlupa. The parish is said to be the oldest in the area, which is why it became the cathedral when the diocese was created.
Accounts of the parish's beginnings differ. Wikipedia says Spanish Augustinian missionaries founded it on

, while another source says a mission station was set up first in 1575 and St. Andrew became the patron saint in 1580. A website that compiles parish information gives 1683 as the year of establishment. For visitors, what matters is that whichever record you follow, this is the heart of one of the oldest faith communities in southern Manila. For an exact year, it is safest to check the parish's own announcements. The original stone church and convent were pulled down in
, along with other churches outside Intramuros, to strengthen Manila's defenses, and the present building is the result of many later rebuildings and renovations.

La Huerta is a small district on the south side of the mouth of the Parañaque River, where it flows into Manila Bay. Its name comes from an orchard (huerta) that stood here in the Spanish era. The Presidencia, the old municipal hall, was built in front of the church in

, and traces of the past remain in the neighborhood, such as St. Andrew's School, which opened in 1917, and the chapel of San Nicolás de Tolentino, built in 1776. The street in front of the church, Quirino Avenue, was once the Calle Real, the royal road.

It is not a flashy tourist attraction, but you get the feel of a neighborhood church, quite different from famous sites such as Manila Cathedral or Intramuros. There is an English Mass at midday on weekdays, and every August and November the cathedral holds major feasts honoring Our Lady and St. Andrew. With the airport nearby and an LRT-1 station within walking distance, it works well for a half-day church tour from Manila or a short stop before or after a flight.

blocks.title: Image of Our Lady of Buen Suceso

children.text: This wooden image of the Virgin and Child at the center of the altar is said to have come from Spain in 1580. After a solemn procession on
August 10, 1625
it was enthroned at this church's altar, and it later received the name Buen Suceso, meaning "Good Event" or "Good Success." Locals affectionately call her "Nana Ciso."
The image received a decree of canonical coronation from Pope John Paul II on
December 18, 1999
, and the coronation took place on
September 8, 2000
. The church was declared a diocesan shrine on
August 10, 2012
, and in September of the same year the Virgin was proclaimed patroness of Parañaque City.

The image of the cathedral's patron, the apostle St. Andrew, is reported (by one source) to be carved from molave wood in the early Spanish colonial style. He is said to stand with his red vestment removed beside his X-shaped cross. It was kept on the church facade for a time, and after restoration it now stands on the right side of the altar (Wikipedia also places it on the right). St. Joseph stands on the left.

The church is described as Baroque in style. A new Baroque-style altar was installed in 1997, and there is a dome that holds the crucifix. You can see the central crucifix, the saints' altars and the altar of Our Lady of Buen Suceso in turn.
The church began a renovation on
January 25, 2009
and blessed the result on

. It is said to have added the bishop's chair, a new organ, a baptismal font and twelve marble stones carved with crosses for the twelve apostles, and there is also a stained-glass window depicting St. Lorenzo Ruiz.

blocks.title: The churchyard and the old district

children.text: In front of the church lies the former site of the Presidencia and Quirino Avenue, the old main street. You can walk to St. Andrew's School and the old riverside streets, so it makes a good short neighborhood stroll rather than ending your visit once you have seen the inside of the church.
Before Our Lady's feast on
August 10
there is a novena from
August 1–9
, and before the feast of St. Andrew on
November 30
there is a novena from
November 21–29
. November 30 is the city's main patronal feast, with a solemn procession. A street-dance event in which local girls dance in front of the church on Easter Sunday is also known.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The church and a stroll through La Huerta

children.text: Get off at LRT-1 Ninoy Aquino station and walk toward the Parañaque River bridge, then on to the church. It is only about
in a straight line.
Look around the facade and the front yard. If Mass is going on, do not walk in; wait quietly at the back or look at the outside first.
Inside, take your time with the image of Our Lady of Buen Suceso on the central altar, the image of St. Andrew on the right and the stained-glass windows.
Walk along Quirino Avenue past St. Andrew's School and through the lanes of the old district.
On weekdays and Saturdays there is an English Mass at
, so attend if the timing suits you. Times can change, so check the parish announcements.
Have lunch at a nearby eatery or at the shopping facilities near the LRT station, then head to your next stop.
You can see the church itself in under an hour. Allow about two hours if you add Mass and a stroll.

items.title: Church pilgrimage route
items.subtitle: Visiting the southern churches by LRT-1

children.text: Start from the Baclaran end of LRT-1. Visit Baclaran Church first, then continue on the same line.
Get off at Ninoy Aquino station and visit St. Andrew Cathedral in Parañaque.
Ride one more stop toward Dr. Santos station and head to the area around St. Joseph Parish, home of the Las Piñas Bamboo Organ. Check locally for how to get there.
If you have time left, look into a visit to the Las Piñas–Parañaque wetland reserve.
All three sites belong to the Diocese of Parañaque. Travel times vary a lot with traffic, so it is better to leave some slack than to squeeze in one more stop.

From central Manila (Ermita or Malate), take LRT-1 toward the southern end of the line. In the Cavite Extension Phase 1, which opened on November 16, 2024, Baclaran is followed by Redemptorist-ASEANA, MIA Road, PITX, Ninoy Aquino and Dr. Santos stations.
Getting off at
Ninoy Aquino station
is the closest option. The station is on Ninoy Aquino Avenue on the east bank of the Parañaque River, and it is about
in a straight line from the church (calculated from the map coordinates of the two places).
Fares depend on the distance, so check the station fare table or LRMC announcements.
Getting from the station to the church means crossing roads and a bridge, so walk with a map app.
Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 1 is close, and you travel along Ninoy Aquino Avenue. A taxi or ride-hailing car is the easiest way.
If you stop at the church only briefly before or after a flight, allow plenty of time for luggage storage and travel. Fares vary with distance and traffic, so check locally.
The distance between the LRT station and the church is walkable, and jeepneys and tricycles run in the area. Jeepney routes such as Baclaran–Sucat are said to connect at the station.
If you go by car or taxi, the Quirino Avenue and Ninoy Aquino Avenue area is congested, so check detours on a map app. Ask the parish whether parking is available.

Since the visit is mostly indoors, rain is not a big problem, but there is some walking, so the dry season is more comfortable. From November to May there is little rain, which makes the walk from the station to the church pleasant.

You can also time your trip to a feast day. On the feast of Our Lady of Buen Suceso on August 10 and the feast of St. Andrew on November 30, events are held and crowds gather. Choose a weekday morning for a quiet visit, or a feast day for the festive atmosphere.

The area around the church is not a place with many tourist lodgings, so most visitors stay at hotels in central Manila or near the airport and visit for half a day. With the airport so close, some travelers stay here before an early flight or after a late arrival, so check the location of your lodging on a map before you book.

Meals are found not in the church but at nearby roadside eateries or the shopping facilities around Ninoy Aquino station. A members-only warehouse store and a duty-free building are known to be near the station. Businesses change often, so check current information on a map app.
During Mass times the church is mainly for worshippers. Look around between Masses, and refrain from photography and loud talking during services.

According to the parish information, weekday Masses are at 6:00 AM, 12:00 noon and 6:00 PM. On Sundays there are several Masses from early morning to evening, so plan your schedule around them. Times may change, so check the parish announcements before you go.
The parish office is said to be open during the day from Tuesday to Saturday and closed on Mondays and holidays. If you need certificates or counseling, check these hours.
Modest clothing that covers your shoulders and knees is the safe choice. Take off your hat when you go in.
If you want to see the image of Our Lady up close, go on a weekday morning when there are fewer people. Feast days are crowded, so watch your belongings.
Combining Baclaran Church and the Las Piñas Bamboo Organ on the same day via LRT-1 makes a rewarding church pilgrimage.
The roads and bridge beside the church have many motorcycles and jeepneys. Be careful when crossing.
Mass times, feast-day events and the hours the church is open may change. Before you go, check the parish announcements or Facebook page.
The founding year differs by source (1575, 1580 and 1683). If you quote it, check the source.
If you stop by before a flight, allow plenty of time for traffic jams.
The streets near the station and the market are crowded, so watch your phone and wallet.
On feast days with processions, roads may be blocked or closed.
The church is a place of worship. Do not photograph worshippers without permission.
A national shrine close by on LRT-1, housing the image of Our Mother of Perpetual Help. It is known for its Wednesday novena.
The bamboo organ at St. Joseph Parish near Dr. Santos station. It belongs to the same diocese, so it combines well into a church pilgrimage.
A wetland on the Manila Bay side where you can see migratory birds. Check the visiting rules locally.
The airport is close to the church, so you can fit the church into a short stop before or after your arrival or departure.
